pos: n. (the northern Irish province settled from Scotland and England after 1609, whose Presbyterian population became the strongest Reformed body in Ireland)
etymology: From Old Norse Ulaðstir, a Norse adaptation of Irish Ulaidh, the people of the north, with the Norse genitive and staðr, a place.
biblical_def: Ulster is the northern province of Ireland, and the most thoroughly settled. After the Nine Years' War ended in 1603 and the northern earls fled in 1607, their lands were declared forfeit and the Plantation of Ulster was organised from 1609: six counties were surveyed and granted to Scottish and English undertakers, to servitors and to the London companies, on condition of settling Protestant tenants, building and keeping arms. Private settlement in Antrim and Down under Hamilton and Montgomery had begun earlier and was larger. By the sixteen-thirties there were tens of thousands of Lowland Scots in the province, with their own ministers, many of them men who had left Scotland over conformity, and the religion of Ulster was Presbyterian rather than episcopal from the start. The rising of 1641 fell on the settlers heavily and was answered in kind. The Presbytery of Ireland was formed at Carrickfergus in 1642 and the Synod of Ulster grew out of it. The dictionary records the plantation as a dispossession and the church that came out of it as genuine, and refuses to let either fact cancel the other.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a plantation as a colony or the place colonised; an undertaker as one who engages in a project; a settler as one who fixes his residence; a stranger as a foreigner; and rest as quiet or repose.
webster_full: PLANTATION, n. The act of planting or settling; a colony; the place planted or settled by emigrants.
UNDERTAKER, n. One who undertakes; one who engages in any project or business; one who covenants to perform.
SETTLER, n. One who settles or establishes himself; one who fixes his residence in a new country; a colonist.
STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one not a native of a place.
REST, n. Cessation of motion or action of any kind; quiet; repose; a state of reconciliation to God.
scriptures: These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,
Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
Act 9:31
Then had the churches rest throughout all Judaea and Galilee and Samaria, and were edified; and walking in the fear of the Lord, and in the comfort of the Holy Ghost, were multiplied.
corruption_summary: Northern Irish province whose lands were declared forfeit after the earls fled in 1607 and planted from 1609 with Scottish and English tenants, producing the strongest Reformed body in Ireland.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the plantation itself considered as policy, and the dictionary names it without pretending that the church which grew out of it was therefore false. Land held by Irish families was declared forfeit by an English administration and granted to strangers on condition that they exclude the previous occupants from the best of it; the Irish were to be tenants at will on the poorer ground or removed. No arrangement of that kind is consistent with the law that secures a man's inheritance, and the dictionary does not improve it by noting that the earls had rebelled or that the settlers were Protestants. What the settlers were in fact, whatever their titles said, is what Hebrews calls every believer: they “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13).

The second paragraph states the duty that followed and the thing that actually came of it. Peter writes to a scattered people as “the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1Pe 1:1), and the charge to men settled in a country not originally theirs is Jeremiah's charge to the exiles, which is neither conquest nor withdrawal: “seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer 29:7). Much of Ulster Presbyterianism did seek the peace of the province, built schools, maintained a learned ministry and in the eighteenth century produced men who argued for the Irish-speaking population rather than against it. The description Luke gives of a church at its best is the dictionary's hope for it: “Then had the churches rest throughout all Judaea and Galilee and Samaria, and were edified; and walking in the fear of the Lord, and in the comfort of the Holy Ghost, were multiplied” (Act 9:31).

pos: n. (the southern Irish province devastated in the Desmond wars and planted from 1586, where some thirty thousand are reckoned to have died of famine)
etymology: From Irish Mumhan, the name of the southern province, with the Norse staðr, a place, giving the English form; distinct from the German city of Münster.
biblical_def: Munster is the southern province of Ireland, comprising Cork, Kerry, Limerick, Clare, Tipperary and Waterford, and in the sixteenth century it was the lordship of the Fitzgeralds, earls of Desmond. Two rebellions, in 1569 and again from 1579, were put down by English forces under Pelham, Ormond and Grey with a deliberate policy of devastation: crops were burned, cattle driven and the country systematically wasted so that the rebels could not be supplied. The result was a famine in which contemporaries reckoned about thirty thousand people died in six months in 1582, and travellers described a province emptied of inhabitants. Edmund Spenser, who held land there and wrote a tract defending the method, recorded what he had seen. The Munster Plantation followed from 1586, granting the forfeited Desmond estates to English undertakers including Raleigh and Boyle. The dictionary records the famine as the deliberate product of a policy and names it so, and it marks the entry as a distinct entity from the German city of the Anabaptist kingdom, which the corpus treats under its own name.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to waste as to lay waste or destroy; a famine as a general scarcity of food; desolation as destruction or ruin; a heritage as an inheritance; and reproach as censure or shame.
webster_full: WASTE, v.t. To diminish by gradual dissipation; to destroy in enmity; to desolate; to lay waste.
FAMINE, n. Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient for the inhabitants of a country.
DESOLATION, n. The act of deserting or laying waste; destruction; ruin; a place laid waste.
HERITAGE, n. Inheritance; an estate that passes from an ancestor to an heir by descent.
REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt; scorn; the cause of shame or disgrace.

Let the priests, the ministers of the LORD, weep between the porch and the altar, and let them say, Spare thy people, O LORD, and give not thine heritage to reproach, that the heathen should rule over them: wherefore should they say among the people, Where is their God?
Lam 2:9
Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars: her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more; her prophets also find no vision from the LORD.
Mic 7:8
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.
Zep 3:12
I will also leave in the midst of thee an afflicted and poor people, and they shall trust in the name of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Southern Irish province and lordship of the Desmonds, wasted by deliberate English policy in the rebellions of 1569 and 1579 with perhaps thirty thousand dead of famine in 1582, and planted from 1586.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the deliberate making of a famine as an instrument of war, and the dictionary names it as murder on a provincial scale. The English commanders in Munster did not merely fail to prevent starvation; they produced it, burning the harvest and driving the cattle on a settled plan so that an armed rising could not be fed, knowing that the people would die first and the rebels after. Spenser defended the policy in print, which removes any question of what was intended. Scripture gives such a province its own prayer, and it is a prayer the dictionary makes on its behalf: “Spare thy people, O LORD, and give not thine heritage to reproach” (Joe 2:17). Lamentations supplies the description of what was left, a country whose “king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more” (Lam 2:9).

The second paragraph is for the people rather than the policy, and the dictionary writes it deliberately, since the sufferers here were overwhelmingly Roman Catholic and the men who wasted their fields called themselves Protestant. That makes no difference to the commandment. Zephaniah describes the kind of remnant God leaves and undertakes to keep, “an afflicted and poor people, and they shall trust in the name of the LORD” (Zep 3:12), and Micah gives the words in which a ruined country may answer those who are pleased with its ruin: “Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me” (Mic 7:8). The dictionary holds that a Reformation advanced by starving a province did not advance it, and that the record of Munster is one of the heaviest charges against the English Protestant settlement in Ireland. The German city whose Anabaptist kingdom bears a similar name is a separate matter and is treated separately.

pos: n. (the western Irish province to which the Cromwellian settlement transplanted the dispossessed Catholic landowners after 1654)
etymology: Irish Connacht, the descendants of Conn, from the legendary Conn Cétchathach; the anglicised form Connaught is also used.
biblical_def: Connacht is the western province of Ireland, comprising Galway, Mayo, Sligo, Roscommon and Leitrim, the poorest and most Irish-speaking of the four. Its place in the dictionary is the Cromwellian settlement. After the reconquest of 1649 to 1653, the Act for the Settling of Ireland and the Act of Satisfaction provided that the estates of Catholic landowners judged to have been in rebellion should be forfeited, that the soldiers and the adventurers who had financed the war should be paid in Irish land, and that such proprietors as were allowed any land at all should receive it in Connacht and Clare, west of the Shannon. Some two thousand families were ordered to transplant by May 1654. The phrase to Hell or Connaught preserves what the transaction looked like to those subjected to it. The province afterwards held a dense Irish-speaking population on poor ground, and the famine of the eighteen-forties fell on it harder than on any other part of Ireland. The dictionary records the transplantation as confiscation under statute and names it so.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to transplant as to remove and plant elsewhere; forfeiture as the loss of property by offence; an adventurer as one who hazards his money; to confiscate as to adjudge to the public treasury; and an inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor.
webster_full: TRANSPLANT, v.t. To remove and plant in another place; to remove and settle or establish for residence.
FORFEITURE, n. The act of forfeiting; the loss of some right, estate or honour, by an offence or crime.
ADVENTURER, n. One who hazards a chance; one who ventures his money in a hazardous enterprise.
CONFISCATE, v.t. To adjudge to be forfeited to the public treasury, as the goods of a criminal.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; a permanent possession.
scriptures: And Naboth said to Ahab, The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee.
Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?
Gen 12:1
Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
corruption_summary: Western Irish province to which the Cromwellian Act of Satisfaction ordered some two thousand dispossessed Catholic landowning families to transplant by May 1654, their estates going to soldiers and adventurers.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is confiscation by statute, and the dictionary names it against a regime many Reformed readers admire. Cromwell's settlement of Ireland was not a riot; it was legislation, with commissioners, surveys, qualifications and a deadline, under which the land of a nation changed hands to pay an army and its creditors. Naboth's refusal states what a family holding is and why no price makes the transfer lawful: “The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee” (1Ki 21:3). Ahab proceeded by a legal form too, and the psalmist's name for government conducted that way is the sharpest in Scripture: “Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?” (Psa 94:20).

The second paragraph distinguishes the two kinds of going out, because Scripture does, and the distinction is the heart of the objection. Abraham was called to leave, and the call came from God with a promise attached: “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee” (Gen 12:1). A family ordered across the Shannon by commissioners under penalty has received no such call and been given no such promise; it has been robbed, and the dictionary will not dress the one in the language of the other. The requirement on every government, Protestant or otherwise, is stated once and is not negotiable: “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8). The dictionary adds that the province so filled was the one the famine of the eighteen-forties afterwards emptied, and that the connection between poor land densely settled by compulsion and a catastrophe two centuries later is not an accident of weather.

pos: n. (the eastern Irish province of Dublin, where Trinity College was founded in 1592 and the Irish New Testament printed in 1602)
etymology: From Irish Laighin, the name of the eastern people, with the Norse staðr, a place, giving the English form.
biblical_def: Leinster is the eastern Irish province, with Dublin at its centre and the Pale about it, and it is where Irish Protestantism did its scholarly work. Trinity College Dublin was founded in 1592 as a seminary for a Protestant ministry; James Ussher entered it as one of its first students, became its professor of divinity and then Archbishop of Armagh, and built the library whose catalogue of Hebrew, Greek and patristic texts was the best in Ireland. The Irish Articles of 1615, drafted largely by Ussher and adopted by the Irish convocation, are more explicitly Calvinist than the Thirty-nine, affirming predestination, reprobation and the perseverance of the saints in terms the English articles leave open. Dublin was also where the Scriptures were put into Irish: William Daniel's Irish New Testament was printed there in 1602 and the Book of Common Prayer in Irish in 1608, and William Bedell, Bishop of Kilmore, had the Old Testament translated by 1640, though it was not printed until 1685. The dictionary records the college, the articles and the Irish Bible together, and holds the third the most important of the three.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a college as a society of men for literary purposes; convocation as an assembly of the clergy; an article as a clause of a confession; a version as a translation; and to prepare as to make ready.
webster_full: COLLEGE, n. A collection or society of men, invested with certain powers, and engaged in some common pursuit, especially literary.
CONVOCATION, n. An assembly; in England, an assembly of the clergy, by their representatives, to consult on ecclesiastical affairs.
ARTICLE, n. A single clause or item of an account, a confession or a charge; a distinct proposition.
VERSION, n. A translation; the act of rendering into another language; as the common version of the Scriptures.
PREPARE, v.t. To fit, adapt or qualify for a particular purpose; to make ready; to provide.
scriptures: Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Ezr 7:10
For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments.
corruption_summary: Eastern Irish province of Dublin and the Pale, where Trinity College was founded in 1592, the Calvinist Irish Articles adopted in 1615, and the Irish New Testament printed in 1602 and the whole Bible by 1685.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the Irish Bible embodies and the one Irish Protestantism most often forgot: that a church sent to a people must speak to them in their own tongue, and that everything else it does is secondary to this. Daniel's New Testament of 1602 and Bedell's Old Testament were the right work. Pentecost is the standard, where the astonishment was that men heard “how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8), and Paul's own preference is for a few intelligible words over a quantity of unintelligible ones: “in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue” (1Co 14:19).

The second thing to recover is the order of a scholar's work, which Ussher at his best exemplified and which his successors did not keep. Ezra's sequence is study, obedience, teaching, and in that order: “For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments” (Ezr 7:10). A college founded to supply a ministry and a convocation that adopted a Calvinist confession were doing the right things; what the establishment largely failed to do was the plainest thing of all, which is to read and open the text to the people in front of it, as at the reading of the law when they “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). Bedell's Old Testament sat in manuscript for forty-five years before anyone printed it, and the dictionary records that delay as the truest measure of how much the Irish establishment wanted the Irish to read.

pos: n. (the north-eastern Irish county where the Six Mile Water revival began at Oldstone about 1625 under the Scottish ministers)
etymology: Irish Aontroim, the lone ridge or single farmstead, from aon, one, and droim, a ridge.
biblical_def: Antrim is the north-eastern Irish county, nearest to Scotland across thirteen miles of water, and the first and heaviest area of Scottish settlement in Ulster; Hamilton and Montgomery were planting tenants in Antrim and Down from 1606, three years before the official plantation. The ministers came with them, and a number of them were men who had left Scotland rather than conform: Edward Brice at Broadisland from 1613, the first Presbyterian minister in Ireland, Robert Cunningham at Holywood, Josias Welsh, grandson of John Knox, at Templepatrick, and James Glendinning at Oldstone near Antrim town. From Glendinning's alarming preaching about 1625 a movement began in the Six Mile Water valley: people were awakened in large numbers, monthly meetings were held at Antrim with several ministers preaching through the day, and Robert Blair of Bangor and John Livingstone of Killinchy were drawn into it. It spread through the settled districts and was the first evangelical revival in Irish Protestant history. The dictionary records it as a work of the Spirit and notes what sustained it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a revival as renewed attention to religion; to awaken as to rouse from sleep or indifference; to breathe as to inspire; conviction as the state of being convinced of sin; and supplication as earnest prayer.
webster_full: REVIVAL, n. Return or recall to life; renewed attention to religion, after indifference and decline.
AWAKEN, v.t. To rouse from sleep; to excite from a state of spiritual indifference or insensibility.
BREATHE, v.t. To inspire or blow into; to infuse by inspiration; to inject by breathing.
CONVICTION, n. The act of convincing, or compelling one to admit the truth of a charge; the state of being convinced of sin.
SUPPLICATION, n. Entreaty; humble and earnest prayer in worship; petition.
scriptures: Act 2:41
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
Joh 3:8
The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.

And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn.
Eze 37:9
Then said he unto me, Prophesy unto the wind, prophesy, son of man, and say to the wind, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live.
corruption_summary: North-eastern Irish county, first and heaviest area of Scottish settlement, where the Six Mile Water revival began at Oldstone about 1625 and spread through the settled districts with monthly meetings at Antrim.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that revival is sovereign in its coming and ordinary in its means. The Six Mile Water work began under a preacher the other ministers thought unbalanced, in a valley of recent immigrants, and it was carried on by catechising, monthly preaching days and the ordinary administration of the sacraments; nothing about it was contrived and nothing about it was irregular either. Our Lord's word about the Spirit governs the first half: “The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh” (Joh 3:8). Luke's record of the first such day gives the second, since “Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls” (Act 2:41).

The second thing to recover is the character of a genuine work, which is mourning before it is rejoicing. The Antrim awakening was marked by deep and sometimes alarming conviction of sin, and its critics then and since have taken that for excess. Zechariah describes the thing God pours out and what it produces, promising “the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him” (Zec 12:10); grace and mourning arrive together. Ezekiel's vision locates the whole operation outside the subjects of it, a prophet commanded to prophesy to the wind and say “Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live” (Eze 37:9). The dictionary records that the ministers of this revival were afterwards deposed by the Irish bishops, that Blair and Livingstone sailed in the Eagle Wing in 1636 attempting New England and were driven back, and that the work in the Six Mile Water valley survived all of it.

pos: n. (the Ulster county of the O'Neills, whose earl's flight in 1607 declared his lands forfeit and opened the Plantation)
etymology: Irish Tír Eóghain, the land of Eóghan, from tír, land, and the personal name of a son of Niall.
biblical_def: Tyrone is the inland Ulster county that was the heartland of the O'Neills, the chief Gaelic dynasty of the north, who were inaugurated at Tullyhogue and claimed the kingship of Ulster. Hugh O'Neill, created Earl of Tyrone by the English and the ablest Irish commander of the age, led the confederacy of the Nine Years' War from 1594, destroyed an English army at the Yellow Ford in 1598, was defeated with his Spanish allies at Kinsale in 1601, and submitted at Mellifont in 1603 days after Elizabeth's death without knowing she was dead. He kept his title and much of his land under the treaty. Four years later, facing prosecution and the steady erosion of his jurisdiction, he and Rory O'Donnell of Tyrconnell took ship from Rathmullan in September 1607 with about ninety followers for the Continent, intending to return with Spanish help; they never came back, O'Neill dying at Rome in 1616. The flight was treated as treason, their lands were declared forfeit, and the Plantation of Ulster followed. The dictionary records the flight as the hinge of Irish history and draws from it the lesson Scripture draws from all such calculations.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to inaugurate as to install with ceremony; forfeit as lost by an offence; to submit as to yield; an ally as one united by treaty; and a lot as that which falls by providence.
webster_full: INAUGURATE, v.t. To introduce or induct into an office with solemnity or suitable ceremonies.
FORFEIT, v.t. To lose by some breach of condition; to lose by some offence, as an estate or a right.
SUBMIT, v.i. To surrender; to yield one's person to the power of another; to be subject.
ALLY, n. A prince or state united by treaty or league; a confederate.
LOT, n. That which, in human speech, is called chance; the decision of providence by casting lots.
scriptures: The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
Jer 17:5
Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.
The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Inland Ulster county and heartland of the O'Neills, whose earl Hugh led the Nine Years' War, submitted in 1603 and took ship from Rathmullan in September 1607, after which the lands were declared forfeit.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the reliance on a foreign Catholic power to settle a domestic quarrel, and the dictionary names it as the error that ruined Gaelic Ulster. O'Neill's war was sustained by Spanish money, Spanish promises and finally a Spanish landing at Kinsale, which obliged him to march the length of Ireland in winter to a battle he need not have fought and lost in an hour; and the flight of 1607 was undertaken on the expectation of a Spanish army that never sailed. Jeremiah's word is written for exactly this calculation: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD” (Jer 17:5). Isaiah's woe on those who go down to Egypt for help is the same judgment in a figure, and so is the psalmist's flat prohibition, “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3).

The second paragraph states what the dictionary will and will not draw from the outcome. That the earls fled, that the lands were forfeited, and that a Protestant population was planted in their place are all under God's hand, since “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” (Pro 16:33). What does not follow is that the Plantation was therefore righteous, or that the English administration which engineered O'Neill's position was vindicated. A providence records a decision of God and settles no argument between men. The duty of preparation remains and so does its limit: “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31). The dictionary notes that the ablest Irish soldier of his century died in Rome waiting on a promise, and that the men who got his land did so by a statute and not by a verdict from heaven.

pos: n. (the Ulster county of the Maguires and the lakes, whose town of Enniskillen held out for William in 1689)
etymology: Irish Fear Manach, the men of Manach, a population group name; the county is dominated by Upper and Lower Lough Erne.
biblical_def: Fermanagh is the Ulster county of Lough Erne, a country of water and drumlins that was the lordship of the Maguires until the Plantation, when it was divided among English and Scottish undertakers and the town of Enniskillen was laid out on its island site between the two lakes. Its moment came in 1689. When James II's Irish army moved north, Enniskillen and Derry were the two Protestant places that did not submit; the Enniskillen men, under Gustavus Hamilton and the rector William Smyth, armed themselves, raised horse and foot, and operated offensively through the summer, defeating a much larger force under Mountcashel at Newtownbutler in July and so relieving the pressure on Derry. William Bedell, the best bishop the Irish establishment produced, had held the neighbouring see of Kilmore from 1629, learned Irish, preached in it and had the Old Testament translated. The dictionary records the defence and then names the thing the entry exists to name, which is the conversion of a deliverance into a permanent identity.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bulwark as a bastion or rampart; a garrison as a body of troops in a fortress; to besiege as to surround with an army; a tower as a lofty building; and deliverance as rescue.
webster_full: BULWARK, n. A bastion; a rampart; a mound of earth or other matter raised for defence.
GARRISON, n. A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town for its defence.
BESIEGE, v.t. To lay siege to; to surround with armed forces; to beset with a view to compel surrender.
TOWER, n. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation; a fortress.
DELIVERANCE, n. Release from captivity, slavery, oppression or any restraint; rescue from danger.
scriptures: Isa 26:1
In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah; We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
corruption_summary: Ulster county of Lough Erne and the Maguires, planted after 1609, whose town of Enniskillen armed itself in 1689 and beat Mountcashel at Newtownbutler in July, relieving the pressure on Derry.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the one Ulster has been most damaged by, and the dictionary names it as a misuse of a real mercy. Enniskillen in 1689 was a genuine deliverance: a small Protestant population, expecting massacre, armed itself and was preserved. What was afterwards done with that memory is another matter. A deliverance commemorated annually becomes a founding story, a founding story becomes an identity, and an identity sanctifies a politics; the siege is then no longer something God did but something a community is. Scripture allows the gladness and relocates the walls. Isaiah's song is sung about a city whose defence is not its masonry: “We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks” (Isa 26:1), and the only tower a man may run into is a name: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10).

The second paragraph names the alternative that was available in the same county and was not followed. William Bedell held Kilmore from 1629, learned Irish in middle age, required his clergy to use it, preached to Irish-speaking congregations and procured the translation of the Old Testament; when the rising came in 1641 the Irish of his diocese protected him and gave him an honourable burial. That is the other way a Protestant minority might have lived in Ireland, and it was tried and it worked. Against the trust that armed men place in their own numbers the psalmist sets the only safe memory: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). And the city a believer is finally told to look for is not any of these, since Abraham “looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10).

pos: n. (the north-western Irish county of the O'Donnells whose Laggan presbytery sent Francis Makemie to found American Presbyterianism)
etymology: Irish Dún na nGall, the fort of the foreigners, from dún, a fort, and Gall, a foreigner, referring to Norse settlers.
biblical_def: Donegal is the north-western Irish county, the old Tyrconnell of the O'Donnells, mountainous and Irish-speaking in the west and settled by Lowland Scots in the eastern district called the Laggan after the Plantation. The Laggan presbytery, formed in 1654 and covering the Scottish settlements of east Donegal and north Tyrone, is the part that concerns the dictionary. It was a working presbytery of a dozen or so ministers under constant legal pressure, meeting, examining and ordaining, and in 1681 it ordained Francis Makemie of Ramelton, a Laggan man educated at Glasgow, in answer to a request for ministers from the Presbyterian settlers of Maryland and Virginia. Makemie went to America, itinerated through the Chesapeake colonies for a quarter of a century, was arrested and tried in New York in 1707 for preaching without a licence and acquitted, and organised in 1706 the Presbytery of Philadelphia, the first on the continent; he is reckoned the father of American Presbyterianism. The dictionary records the ordination as the single most consequential act a small Irish presbytery ever performed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a presbytery as a body of elders; to ordain as to set apart for an office; to itinerate as to travel from place to place; to enlarge as to extend in limits; and to sound as to be spread abroad.
webster_full: PRESBYTERY, n. A body of elders in the Christian church; a judicatory consisting of the ministers and elders of a district.
ORDAIN, v.t. To set apart for an office; to appoint; to invest with ministerial functions by the laying on of hands.
ITINERATE, v.i. To travel from place to place, particularly for the purpose of preaching.
ENLARGE, v.t. To make greater in quantity or dimensions; to extend in limits, breadth or size.
SOUND, v.i. To make a noise; to be conveyed in sound; to be spread or published.
scriptures: Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Isa 54:2
Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes;
For from you sounded out the word of the Lord not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith to God-ward is spread abroad; so that we need not to speak any thing.
corruption_summary: North-western Irish county of the O'Donnells whose Laggan presbytery, formed in 1654, ordained Francis Makemie of Ramelton in 1681 for the Chesapeake, where he organised the first American presbytery in 1706.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an ordination is an act of the whole church and that a small body under pressure may send further than a large one at ease. The Laggan presbytery had a dozen ministers, no legal standing, and magistrates who fined and imprisoned them; it nevertheless kept records, examined candidates and, on a letter from planters in Maryland, laid hands on a young man and sent him across an ocean. The apostolic pattern for how the Gospel actually spreads is a scattering rather than a strategy, since “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4); and the commission that authorised the Laggan men to think in such terms admits no boundary, “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15).

The second thing to recover is the condition attached to enlargement, which Isaiah states in a single image and which the Laggan presbytery met. The command is to spread out and in the same breath to make the holding deeper: “Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes” (Isa 54:2); a church that sends without ordaining, examining and holding its men to a confession is stretching cords over loose pegs. Makemie went out ordained by a presbytery to a confession, which is why what he founded held. Paul's commendation of a sending church is the dictionary's verdict on this one: “from you sounded out the word of the Lord not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith to God-ward is spread abroad” (1Th 1:8). A dozen harassed ministers in east Donegal furnished a continent with a church order, and the dictionary counts that the best answer available to any congregation which thinks itself too small to matter.

pos: n. (the walled Protestant town founded in County Cork in 1604, whose exclusion of Catholics became a byword)
etymology: From the river Bandon, Irish Abha Bhandan, of uncertain sense; the town is Droichead na Bandan, the bridge of the Bandon.
biblical_def: Bandon is the town in County Cork founded in 1604 by English settlers under the patronage of Richard Boyle, afterwards Earl of Cork, as a wholly Protestant plantation borough. It was walled at great expense by 1625, with three gates and a circuit nearly a mile round, and its charter and town rules excluded Catholics from residence and from trade within the walls; the local tradition that an inscription over the gate declared that Turk, Jew or atheist might enter there but not a papist is almost certainly a later invention, but it records accurately what the town was for. Bandon prospered as a cloth and brewing town, was held against the Irish in 1641 and 1642, and declared for William in 1689 before the main war reached Munster. The dictionary enters Bandon to name a corruption which is not Roman and not liberal but specifically our own: the conversion of a confession of faith into a wall and a residence qualification, so that Protestantism becomes a matter of who may live in a street.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a borough as a corporate town; a charter as a written instrument of privileges; to exclude as to shut out; zeal as ardour in pursuit of an object; and winsome's root, to win, as to gain by persuasion.
webster_full: BOROUGH, n. A town with a corporation; a corporate town that is not a city.
CHARTER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant or privilege.
EXCLUDE, v.t. To thrust out; to hinder from entering or admission; to debar from participation.
ZEAL, n. Passionate ardour in the pursuit of any thing; ardent and eager desire, in a good or bad cause.
WIN, v.t. To gain by success in competition or contest; to gain by persuasion or influence.
scriptures: Rom 10:2
For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
Luk 9:55
But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.
Jam 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
corruption_summary: Walled Protestant plantation borough founded in County Cork in 1604 under Richard Boyle, whose charter and town rules excluded Catholics from residence and trade within its mile of wall.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is ours, and the dictionary names it as the exact inversion of the Reformation's own claim. The Reformers argued that the church is gathered by the Word, that faith cannot be compelled and that a man is justified by believing and not by belonging. Bandon turned that into a residence qualification: the walls kept out a religion, the charter kept out its adherents, and to be a Protestant in that town meant to be inside something. Paul's judgment on zeal of the wrong kind is the judgment here, and he passes it on men whose zeal was real: “I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2). A mile of wall is zeal; it is not knowledge, and it converted nobody.

The second paragraph states what a town so founded could not do and what it therefore became. A congregation that defines itself by exclusion must keep finding people to exclude, and its religion gradually consists of the boundary. Our Lord's rebuke to disciples who proposed to destroy an unreceptive village is the standing word against the whole temper: “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55). James removes the plea that the cause justified it, since “the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jam 1:20); and where an observance rests on a town's custom rather than on God's command it falls under the word spoken to the Pharisees, “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9). The dictionary notes that Bandon's walls were useful in 1641 and that the lives they saved were real; and that a church which can only preserve itself by excluding its neighbours from the street has given up the only method it was ever given.

pos: n. (the Antrim castle town where the chaplains of the Scottish army constituted the first presbytery in Ireland in June 1642)
etymology: Irish Carraig Fhearghais, the rock of Fergus, from carraig, a rock, and the personal name.
biblical_def: Carrickfergus is the Antrim town on Belfast Lough, dominated by the Norman castle that was for centuries the chief English stronghold in the north of Ireland. Its place in the dictionary is one meeting. After the rising of 1641 a Scottish army under Major-General Robert Monro was sent to Ulster, and with it came regimental chaplains and elders; in June 1642, at Carrickfergus, these chaplains and elders constituted themselves a presbytery, the first in Ireland. They were asked almost at once for help by the scattered Scottish congregations of Antrim and Down, which had been without settled ministers since the bishops deposed their preachers in the sixteen-thirties, and they began to supply, ordain and organise. From that presbytery the Presbyterian Church in Ireland descends, and within forty years it had five presbyteries and a synod. The town was also where William III landed in June 1690 on his way to the Boyne. The dictionary records the 1642 meeting and states the principle that an army chaplaincy stumbled on, which is that a presbytery is constituted by ministers and elders and not by a king, a bishop or a parliament.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a presbytery as a body of elders; a chaplain as a clergyman attached to a regiment or household; to constitute as to set up or establish; to ordain as to invest with ministerial function; and order as methodical arrangement.
webster_full: PRESBYTERY, n. A body of elders in the Christian church; a judicatory consisting of ministers and elders.
CHAPLAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who has the care of a chapel; a clergyman who belongs to a ship of war, a regiment or a family.
CONSTITUTE, v.t. To set; to fix; to establish; to form or compose; to appoint or elect to an office.
ORDAIN, v.t. To set apart for an office; to invest with ministerial functions by the laying on of hands.
ORDER, n. Regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things; settled mode of proceeding.
scriptures: Act 15:2

When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Antrim castle town where the chaplains and elders of Monro's Scottish army constituted the first presbytery in Ireland in June 1642, from which the Presbyterian Church in Ireland descends.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a presbytery is constituted by the men Christ has given to His church and not by any civil or prelatical authority. The Carrickfergus meeting had no warrant from a king, no licence from a bishop and no act of parliament; it had ministers lawfully ordained, elders lawfully chosen, and a people asking to be supplied, and that was enough. The apostolic precedent is a council of ministers and elders deliberating a question referred to them, where Paul and Barnabas and others went “up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question” (Act 15:2). The thing such a body exists to maintain is set out as four continuing practices: “And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42).

The second thing to recover is that order of this kind is a duty and not a preference. Titus was left in Crete with a specific commission to supply what was lacking, which is exactly what the Carrickfergus presbytery found itself doing for the deserted congregations of Antrim and Down: “For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5). Paul's closing rule for an assembly that had been running on gifts without arrangement is the rule a presbytery exists to apply: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). The dictionary notes the irony it is bound to note: the first presbytery in Ireland was gathered by the chaplains of an invading army in a war it does not defend, and what they constituted outlasted the army, the war, the castle's garrison and the establishment that had deposed their predecessors.
